passage:
The white kurta came out of the hostel washing machine pink. Nikita held it up in the laundry room, hot with anger at herself. She had thrown in a red scarf with it because there were three loads and she was tired. Her roommates' shirts hung neatly on the line. She almost buried the kurta at the bottom of her cupboard. Instead she carried it downstairs to Naveen bhaiya, the hostel caretaker, who was fixing a tap. "I ruined it."
He glanced at it and smiled. "Every first-year does. Colours apart, cold water, and ask the girls upstairs about good soap."
She wrote "colours apart" on her palm. Then she asked her roommate Divya how she planned her month's money, because Nikita's own budget was already thin.

qa.q: What did Nikita throw in the wash together with the white kurta?
qa.a: She threw in a red scarf.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling in the laundry room?
qa.a: She felt angry with herself for the mistake, and perhaps a little embarrassed, since she almost hid the kurta in her cupboard.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene turned the mistake into a lesson?
qa.a: She chose to show the pink kurta to Naveen bhaiya instead of hiding it, and then asked her roommate about money planning as well.

qa.q: How does Naveen bhaiya seem to see Nikita's mistake?
qa.a: He treats it as ordinary, saying every first-year does it, and uses it to teach her simple laundry habits instead of scolding her.

grounding: A student handling laundry and money alone for the first time learns from a mistake by asking for help.

passage:
Dear Suraj bhaiya,

The room is smaller than the photo: four beds and one table for four strangers. Last week I was so angry when Mitali switched on the tube light at five in the morning that I said nothing all day, which was worse. Then we talked, and now the lights go off at eleven.

Money is my other lesson. I spent most of the month's allowance in the first two weeks on books and outside food, and by the third week I was counting coins. I felt too proud to tell Papa. Instead I asked a hostel senior how they plan mess coupons, and they showed me a small notebook system. Asking was not as bad as I thought.

Write back and tell me your first-year mistakes.

Neelam

qa.q: At what time did Mitali switch on the tube light?
qa.a: Mitali switched it on at five in the morning.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when the tube light came on?
qa.a: Neelam was angry, so angry that the whole day passed in silence.

qa.q: What two steps did Neelam take to fix the problems in the hostel?
qa.a: Neelam talked with the roommates so the lights now go off at eleven, and asked a hostel senior how to plan mess coupons and money.

qa.q: What might Mitali have thought when Neelam stayed silent all day, and what changed after they talked?
qa.a: Mitali may have been confused or uneasy about the silence; after the talk, the lights went off at eleven, so the problem had a clear fix.

grounding: A student sharing a room with strangers and managing money alone treats mistakes as lessons and asks for help.

passage:
Jomon, you asked about my first semester in the hostel? Okay, it was a disaster, but a useful one.
First, I shrank every piece of clothing I owned. I put everything in hot water, even my woollen sweater. It came out doll-sized.
Second, I ran out of money by the twentieth, because I kept ordering food at night. I was too proud to tell Papa.
Third, my roommate played music till two every night, and one day I just exploded at him. We didn't speak for a week.
Then a senior, Naina Didi, found me eating dry biscuits for dinner. She said, "Everyone messes up first year. Asking for help isn't weak." She showed me how to make a monthly budget, and she helped me talk to my roommate calmly.
So that's Ankita's hostel story. Now I'm the one teaching juniors how to wash sweaters.

qa.q: What happened to Ankita's woollen sweater?
qa.a: It came out doll-sized.

qa.q: Why didn't Ankita tell Papa she'd run out of money?
qa.a: Ankita felt too proud and embarrassed to admit the mistake.

qa.q: What turned things around for Ankita?
qa.a: Accepting help from Naina Didi, who showed Ankita how to budget and helped with a calm talk with the roommate, turned mistakes into lessons.

qa.q: How might the roommate have felt when Ankita exploded at him?
qa.a: The roommate was probably surprised and defensive, and may not have known how much the music bothered Ankita.

grounding: A student recalls first hostel mistakes with laundry, money and a roommate, and learning that asking for help is a strength.

passage:
Week one. Chetan, eighteen, shared a hostel room in Bhopal with two strangers. One snored; the other, Santosh, left wet towels on Chetan's bed. By Friday Chetan had overspent his month's money on canteen food.
Week three. Chetan came back to find his laptop charger borrowed again. He shouted at Santosh, "Can't you ask first?" Santosh shouted back. Chetan went to the terrace, furious and ashamed. He hadn't eaten a proper meal in days.
Week five. Chetan went to the warden's office and admitted everything: the money, the fights. The warden didn't lecture. She helped him set a weekly budget and suggested a room meeting. That evening, the three roommates wrote rules on a paper: ask before borrowing, towels on hooks, lights off at midnight. Santosh added, "Sorry about the charger." Chetan laughed. "Sorry about the shouting."

qa.q: What did Santosh leave on Chetan's bed?
qa.a: Santosh left wet towels on Chetan's bed.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on the terrace in week three?
qa.a: Chetan felt furious and ashamed after shouting, and was tired and hungry.

qa.q: Why was going to the warden a strength, not a failure?
qa.a: Admitting the mistakes let the warden help him set a budget and organise a room meeting, which fixed the problems instead of letting them grow.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt when the rules were written?
qa.a: Santosh seemed relieved and sorry, which is why he apologised about the charger.

grounding: Over several weeks, a student sharing a hostel room struggles with money and anger, then asks for help and learns from mistakes.

passage:
Ojas, you're thinking of leaving the hostel because you messed up your mess money? Let your Pradeep Kaka tell you about 1989.
I was nineteen, in the hostel at Jadavpur. My father sent a money order on the first of every month. By the tenth, it was gone: cinema, snacks, lending to friends who never paid back. For two weeks I lived on bread and tea.
I was too ashamed to tell anyone. I got angry at everyone, my roommates, the mess manager, myself.
Then the mess manager, a gruff old man called Haldar Babu, saw me skipping meals. He said, "Eat now, pay when the money comes. And come see me; I'll show you how to write every paisa in a notebook."
I kept that notebook for forty years. The turning point wasn't the money, Ojas. It was letting someone help.

qa.q: What was the mess manager called?
qa.a: He was a gruff old man called Haldar Babu.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel during the two weeks of bread and tea?
qa.a: Pradeep felt ashamed and angry at everyone, including himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pradeep's story?
qa.a: The turning point was letting Haldar Babu help him, eating on credit and learning to write every paisa in a notebook.

qa.q: How might Haldar Babu have seen young Pradeep?
qa.a: Haldar Babu probably saw a struggling boy too proud to ask, and felt concern beneath his gruffness.

grounding: An elder recalls his first hostel year, running out of money and getting angry, and learning that asking for help is a strength.

passage: The water in Block C went off on the Monday of Gautam's first exam week, and he had one clean shirt left. He had shrunk the other two in the hostel machine on the hot cycle. His roommates, strangers from Assam and Kerala, were still asleep. He had also spent most of his monthly allowance in the first fortnight on canteen parathas. At seven he found his lab partner Damini hanging washing on the line outside the girls' block. "How do you make the money last?" he asked, embarrassed. Damini laughed kindly. "The mess is cheaper than the canteen. And cold wash, always. Everyone ruins shirts in first year." That night Gautam asked his roommates to share a bucket of water from the tanker. They ended up cooking instant noodles on a borrowed kettle and finally learnt each other's names properly.

qa.q: How did Gautam shrink his shirts?
qa.a: He shrank them in the hostel machine on the hot cycle.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel asking Damini for help?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his mistakes, yet trusted Damini enough to ask, and was likely relieved by her kind laugh.

qa.q: What does Gautam's week show about hostel mistakes?
qa.a: Mistakes like shrunken shirts and a thin wallet turn into lessons once he asks for help, from Damini and from his roommates.

qa.q: How might Gautam's roommates see him after the water cut?
qa.a: They probably find him friendlier and easier to live with, since his asking to share water led to cooking together and learning names.

grounding: It illustrates a student handling laundry, food and money alone for the first time in a shared room, learning from mistakes and finding that asking for help is a strength.
